definition: Inserted into the calendar to reconcile it with the solar year; by extension, anything inserted between regular intervals to restore balance or fill a gap.
etymology: From Latin intercalaris, built on intercalare — to proclaim the insertion of an extra day or month. The Romans would shout cal! (from calare, to call out) at the new moon to announce the month's beginning; intercalating meant slipping something in between those cries to keep civic and cosmic time from drifting apart.
usage: June once sat near the great intercalary anxieties of the Roman calendar — leap adjustments that priests could manipulate for political ends. Use it today for any corrective insertion: an intercalary chapter that bridges two eras, an intercalary rest day sewn into a punishing schedule.
